Job asks his friends to listen (verses 1–6)

Job came directly to the central issue.

Does outward prosperity prove that someone belongs to God's true people, so that the loss of prosperity proves hypocrisy?

His friends answered yes. Job answered no.

Anyone looking at Job could see enough suffering to deserve sympathy.

Instead of speaking with such certainty about God's mysterious purposes, his friends should have responded with reverent silence and wonder.

Wicked people may prosper (verses 7–16)

Job observed that notorious sinners sometimes experience extraordinary judgments, but not always.

Why does God allow some wicked people to prosper?

This is a time of divine patience.

God can use even the prosperity of ungodly people to carry out his plans, while their unrepentance moves them toward destruction.

Another reason is to show clearly that there is a world beyond this one.

Some wealthy sinners disregard God and religion, imagining that because they have everything they want in this world, they have no need to consider the next.

Yet true religion is not empty.

If it brings us no benefit, we may have only embraced its outward appearance without its living reality.

Job exposed the folly of such confidence.

Providence deals differently with different sinners (verses 17–26)

Job contrasted wicked people's prosperity with his friends' assertion that they must always be visibly ruined in this life.

This did not contradict God's holiness or justice.

Even when wicked people prosper, their condition remains spiritually empty.

Their power and splendor can disappear in a moment.

Why one evil person enjoys a longer period of prosperity while another suffers early belongs to God's wisdom.

He is the Judge of the whole earth, and he will act justly.

Time is so brief compared with eternity that earthly differences become small in view of final judgment.

If hell is the final lot of unrepentant sinners, it makes little difference whether one goes there singing and another sighing.

Whether one dies in a palace and another in a prison, the worm that does not die and the fire that is not quenched are the same for both.

We should therefore avoid becoming consumed with questions about why earthly fortunes differ.

Judgment awaits beyond the grave (verses 27–34)

Job rejected the idea that all wicked people must suffer a visible and dramatic fall in this life, and that only wicked people suffer such a fall.

This was the false assumption his friends used to condemn him.

The full punishment of unrepentant sinners belongs chiefly to the world to come, not necessarily to present life (Jude 1:14–15).

A wicked person may retain power until death and receive a magnificent funeral.

But what is there to boast about in that?

A splendid tomb and a beautiful burial place with water to keep its grass green were considered honorable in the ancient East.

They are still empty earthly distinctions.

Death brings worldly prosperity to an end.

The fact that others died before us is little comfort when we ourselves approach death.

True courage at that hour comes from remembering that Jesus Christ died and was buried not only before us but for us.

He went ahead of us, died for us and now lives for us.

That is genuine comfort in the hour of death.

[Job.21.1-Job.21.6]
Chapter 21
Chapter Outline
Job entreats attention. | (1-6) |
The prosperity of the wicked. | (7-16) |
The dealings of God's providence. | (17-26) |
The judgement of the wicked is in the world to come. | (27-34) |
Verses 1-6
Job comes closer to the question in dispute. This was, Whether outward prosperity is a mark of the true church, and the true members of it, so that ruin of a man's prosperity proves him a hypocrite? This they asserted, but Job denied. If they looked upon him, they might see misery enough to demand compassion, and their bold interpretations of this mysterious providence should be turned into silent wonder.
[Job.21.7-Job.21.16]
Verses 7-16
Job says, Remarkable judgments are sometimes brought upon notorious sinners, but not always. Wherefore is it so? This is the day of God's patience; and, in some way or other, he makes use of the prosperity of the wicked to serve his own counsels, while it ripens them for ruin; but the chief reason is, because he will make it appear there is another world. These prospering sinners make light of God and religion, as if because they have so much of this world, they had no need to look after another. But religion is not a vain thing. If it be so to us, we may thank ourselves for resting on the outside of it. Job shows their folly.
[Job.21.17-Job.21.26]
Verses 17-26
Job had described the prosperity of wicked people; in these verses he opposes this to what his friends had maintained about their certain ruin in this life. He reconciles this to the holiness and justice of God. Even while they prosper thus, they are light and worthless, of no account with God, or with wise men. In the height of their pomp and power, there is but a step between them and ruin. Job refers the difference Providence makes between one wicked man and another, into the wisdom of God. He is Judge of all the earth, and he will do right. So vast is the disproportion between time and eternity, that if hell be the lot of every sinner at last, it makes little difference if one goes singing thither, and another sighing. If one wicked man die in a palace, and another in a dungeon, the worm that dies not, and the fire that is not quenched, will be the same to them. Thus differences in this world are not worth perplexing ourselves about.
[Job.21.27-Job.21.34]
Verses 27-34
Job opposes the opinion of his friends, That the wicked are sure to fall into visible and remarkable ruin, and none but the wicked; upon which principle they condemned Job as wicked. Turn to whom you will, you will find that the punishment of sinners is designed more for the other world than for this, [Jude.1.14] Jude 1:14, [1Cor.1.15] 15. The sinner is here supposed to live in a great deal of power. The sinner shall have a splendid funeral: a poor thing for any man to be proud of the prospect of. He shall have a stately monument. And a valley with springs of water to keep the turf green, was accounted an honourable burial place among eastern people; but such things are vain distinctions. Death closes his prosperity. It is but a poor encouragement to die, that others have died before us. That which makes a man die with true courage, is, with faith to remember that Jesus Christ died and was laid in the grave, not only before us, but for us. That He hath gone before us, and died for us, who is alive and liveth for us, is true consolation in the hour of death.

Eliphaz says God gains nothing from human goodness (verses 1–4)

Eliphaz misunderstood Job's complaints as an accusation that God was unjust to afflict him.

Job had not actually meant that.

Eliphaz's teachings here were wrongly applied to Job, yet their main principle was true.

God is not indebted to us when he gives us good things.

Human godliness does not enrich him or provide something he lacks.

The benefit of religion to human beings is infinitely greater than any loss we sustain through obedience.

God is sovereign and does not have to justify his choices to created beings.

Nevertheless, his character is entirely wise, righteous, faithful, good and merciful.

He delights in holiness that reflects his own character and in the fruit of his Spirit.

He accepts the humble believer's grateful service but rejects the proud claims of people who think their goodness earns his favor.

Eliphaz accuses Job of oppressing others (verses 5–14)

Eliphaz leveled serious accusations against Job.

He had no real grounds for them except his belief that God must have punished Job as he always punishes wicked people.

Eliphaz therefore charged Job with using his former wealth and influence to harm and oppress others.

Henry presents these statements as baseless accusations, not as facts about Job.

Eliphaz invokes the people before the flood (verses 15–20)

Eliphaz asked Job to consider the ancient paths of wicked people and the destruction toward which they led.

That history is a warning we should study so we do not follow the same path.

But when others suffer and we are spared, we must not boast over them or congratulate ourselves, as Eliphaz did.

We ought instead to thank God for mercy and take the events as warnings to ourselves.

Eliphaz tells Job to repent (verses 21–30)

Eliphaz's counsel wrongly implied that Job had never truly known God and that conversion would necessarily restore his worldly prosperity.

Much of the counsel was good in itself.

But its application was based on the false supposition that Job was a stranger and enemy to God.

We must avoid slandering our brothers and sisters.

If we suffer unjust accusations, remember Job's treatment—and even more, how Jesus was insulted.

These examples can strengthen our patience.

We should still examine whether any part of the criticism has merit.

Let us live carefully and avoid even the appearance of wrongdoing.

Verses 1-4
Eliphaz considers that, because Job complained so much of his afflictions, he thought God was unjust in afflicting him; but Job was far from thinking so. What Eliphaz says, is unjustly applied to Job, but it is very true, that when God does us good it is not because he is indebted to us. Man's piety is no profit to God, no gain. The gains of religion to men are infinitely greater than the losses of it. God is a Sovereign, who gives no account of his conduct; but he is perfectly wise, just, faithful, good, and merciful. He approves the likeness of his own holiness, and delights in the fruits of his Spirit; he accepts the thankful services of the humble believer, while he rejects the proud claim of the self-confident.
[Job.22.5-Job.22.14]
Verses 5-14
Eliphaz brought heavy charges against Job, without reason for his accusations, except that Job was visited as he supposed God always visited every wicked man. He charges him with oppression, and that he did harm with his wealth and power in the time of his prosperity.
[Job.22.15-Job.22.20]
Verses 15-20
Eliphaz would have Job mark the old way that wicked men have trodden, and see what the end of their way was. It is good for us to mark it, that we may not walk therein. But if others are consumed, and we are not, instead of blaming them, and lifting up ourselves, as Eliphaz does here, we ought to be thankful to God, and take it for a warning.
[Job.22.21-Job.22.30]
Verses 21-30
The answer of Eliphaz wrongly implied that Job had hitherto not known God, and that prosperity in this life would follow his sincere conversion. The counsel Eliphaz here gives is good, though, as to Job, it was built upon a false supposition that he was a stranger and enemy to God. Let us beware of slandering our brethren; and if it be our lot to suffer in this manner, let us remember how Job was treated; yea, how Jesus was reviled, that we may be patient. Let us examine whether there may not be some colour for the slander, and walk watchfully, so as to be clear of all appearances of evil.

Job longs to bring his case before God (verses 1–7)

Job appealed from his friends to God's righteous judgment.

He wanted his case to be heard immediately.

Blessed be God: we know where we can find him.

He is in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, and sits upon a throne of mercy, ready to show grace.

There the sinner may come.

There the believer may present a case and plead on the basis of God's promises, his covenant and his glory.

Patiently waiting for death and judgment is wise and right, accompanied by holy reverence.

Passionately demanding that they come immediately is sinful and foolish.

Such impatience was unworthy of Job.

Job speaks of his upright conduct (verses 8–12)

Job knew the Lord was present everywhere.

But his distress confused his thinking so badly that he could not grasp God's merciful presence or find comfort in laying his troubles before him.

Everything seemed dark.

He felt that God stood far away and looked on him with displeasure.

Nevertheless, Job believed that God would test him and finally approve him, because he had sought to keep God's commands and delighted in his word.

Yet here he was justifying himself more than God, even against God (Job 32:2).

Job was right to reject the baseless charges of his friends.

But he was wrong to assert so confidently that God's affliction could not involve discipline for sin.

Henry also finds a second mistake: Job appeared to deny that Providence sometimes brings justice to injured people or punishes wickedness in this present world.

Job trembles before God's sovereignty (verses 13–17)

Job never doubted that his trials came under God's hand.

He did not believe in blind chance.

How then did he understand them?

He emphasized that the complete reward of God's servants lies in another life, since wicked people often escape their deserved consequences on earth.

Yet God's grace already gives believers a first taste of the Spirit and a promise that God will complete the good work he has begun.

A suffering believer should not conclude that prayer is useless or that despair is justified.

God may intend the affliction to awaken repentance and prayer.

May we obey and trust him amid suffering and remain willing to live or die according to his will.

We do not know what good purposes may be served by extending or shortening our earthly lives.

[Job.23.1-Job.23.7]
Chapter 23
Chapter Outline
Job complains that God has withdrawn. | (1-7) |
He asserts his own integrity. | (8-12) |
The Divine terrors. | (13-17) |
Verses 1-7
Job appeals from his friends to the just judgement of God. He wants to have his cause tried quickly. Blessed be God, we may know where to find him. He is in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself; and upon a mercy-seat, waiting to be gracious. Thither the sinner may go; and there the believer may order his cause before Him, with arguments taken from his promises, his covenant, and his glory. A patient waiting for death and judgment is our wisdom and duty, and it cannot be without a holy fear and trembling. A passionate wishing for death or judgement is our sin and folly, and ill becomes us, as it did Job.
[Job.23.8-Job.23.12]
Verses 8-12
Job knew that the Lord was every where present; but his mind was in such confusion, that he could get no fixed view of God's merciful presence, so as to find comfort by spreading his case before him. His views were all gloomy. God seemed to stand at a distance, and frown upon him. Yet Job expressed his assurance that he should be brought forth, tried, and approved, for he had obeyed the precepts of God. He had relished and delighted in the truths and commandments of God. Here we should notice that Job justified himself rather than God, or in opposition to him, ch. 32:2. Job might feel that he was clear from the charges of his friends, but boldly to assert that, though visited by the hand of God, it was not a chastisement of sin, was his error. And he is guilty of a second, when he denies that there are dealings of Providence with men in this present life, wherein the injured find redress, and the evil are visited for their sins.
[Job.23.13-Job.23.17]
Verses 13-17
As Job does not once question but that his trials are from the hand of God, and that there is no such thing as chance, how does he account for them? The principle on which he views them is, that the hope and reward of the faithful servants of God are only laid up in another life; and he maintains that it is plain to all, that the wicked are not treated according to their deserts in this life, but often directly the reverse. But though the obtaining of mercy, the first-fruits of the Spirit of grace, pledges a God, who will certainly finish the work which he has began; yet the afflicted believer is not to conclude that all prayer and entreaty will be in vain, and that he should sink into despair, and faint when he is reproved of Him. He cannot tell but the intention of God in afflicting him may be to produce penitence and prayer in his heart. May we learn to obey and trust the Lord, even in tribulation; to live or die as he pleases: we know not for what good ends our lives may be shortened or prolonged.

Wickedness may go unpunished for a time (verses 1–12)

Job continued discussing the prosperity of wicked people.

He had already shown in chapter 21 that people who disregard God can live comfortably.

Here he observed that some who openly defy justice succeed in their wicked actions without receiving visible punishment in this life.

He considered both those who act unjustly under the cover of law and authority and robbers who use force.

Job said that God did not immediately call them to account for their folly.

He did not mean God failed to see their deeds.

He meant that judgment did not come at once, exposing them publicly as foolish.

Yet the person who becomes rich through injustice will finally be exposed as a fool (Jeremiah 17:11).

Wicked people avoid the light (verses 13–17)

Consider the energy and effort sinners invest in carrying out harmful plans.

Their determination should shame our laziness about doing what is good.

They work hard to indulge sinful desires and then to conceal what will end in death and hell.

With less effort than they spend pursuing and hiding sin, they could instead put sinful desires to death and crucify the flesh—the path leading to life and heaven.

Shame entered the world through sin, and lasting shame awaits those who persist in it.

Sinners live with constant fear of being discovered.

How foolish!

They are afraid of human eyes, yet they do not fear the eye of God, which always sees them.

They are not frightened of committing deeds they are terrified others may discover.

Job reflects on the judgments of the wicked (verses 18–25)

Some wicked people decline gradually and die quietly.

They may be honored in life and forgotten after death, along with their violence and oppression.

Death gathers people as a harvest worker gathers ears of grain.

Some of Job's observations may appear to match what we see in Providence.

But Henry warns that Job's conclusions about God's purposes were distorted by partial knowledge.

The Lord governs human affairs with complete justice and wisdom.

We must remember this whenever he tests us.

God cannot do wrong.

The unequaled suffering of God's Son would seem puzzling if viewed apart from this truth.

But when we see Christ as the sinner's Surety, bearing the curse we deserved, we understand how divine justice could be satisfied and his people saved through such suffering.

Verses 1-12
Job discourses further about the prosperity of the wicked. That many live at ease who are ungodly and profane, he had showed, ch. xxi. Here he shows that many who live in open defiance of all the laws of justice, succeed in wicked practices; and we do not see them reckoned with in this world. He notices those that do wrong under pretence of law and authority; and robbers, those that do wrong by force. He says, "God layeth not folly to them;" that is, he does not at once send his judgments, nor make them examples, and so manifest their folly to all the world. But he that gets riches, and not by right, at his end shall be a fool, [Jer.17.11] Jer 17:11.
[Job.24.13-Job.24.17]
Verses 13-17
See what care and pains wicked men take to compass their wicked designs; let it shame our negligence and slothfulness in doing good. See what pains those take, who make provision for the flesh to fulfil the lusts of it: pains to compass, and then to hide that which will end in death and hell at last. Less pains would mortify and crucify the flesh, and be life and heaven at last. Shame came in with sin, and everlasting shame is at the end of it. See the misery of sinners; they are exposed to continual frights: yet see their folly; they are afraid of coming under the eye of men, but have no dread of God's eye, which is always upon them: they are not afraid of doing things which they are afraid of being known to do.
[Job.24.18-Job.24.25]
Verses 18-25
Sometimes how gradual is the decay, how quiet the departure of a wicked person, how is he honoured, and how soon are all his cruelties and oppressions forgotten! They are taken off with other men, as the harvestman gathers the ears of corn as they come to hand. There will often appear much to resemble the wrong view of Providence Job takes in this chapter. But we are taught by the word of inspiration, that these notions are formed in ignorance, from partial views. The providence of God, in the affairs of men, is in every thing a just and wise providence. Let us apply this whenever the Lord may try us. He cannot do wrong. The unequalled sorrows of the Son of God when on earth, unless looked at in this view, perplex the mind. But when we behold him, as the sinner's Surety, bearing the curse, we can explain why he should endure that wrath which was due to sin, that Divine justice might be satisfied, and his people saved.

Original heading

Bildad shows that man cannot be justified before God.

Bildad considers human impurity before God

Bildad no longer discussed the question of why wicked people sometimes prosper.

Instead, he spoke of the immense distance between God's glory and human beings' weakness.

He reminded Job of truths Job had not considered sufficiently.

Even human righteousness and holiness at their best are nothing compared with God's holiness (Psalm 89:6).

How can guilty and polluted people stand before a God so glorious and great?

We must be born again by water and the Holy Spirit.

We must continually turn to the blood of Jesus Christ, the fountain opened to cleanse sin (Zechariah 13:1).

Let us humble ourselves as weak and sinful creatures and abandon every confidence in our own merit.

Yet awareness of our unworthiness makes Christ's condescension and love shine even more brightly.

Every sinner he redeems will eternally glorify the riches of his mercy and the power of his grace.

[Job.25.1]
Chapter 25
Bildad shows that man cannot be justified before God.
--Bildad drops the question concerning the prosperity of wicked men; but shows the infinite distance there is between God and man. He represents to Job some truths he had too much overlooked. Man's righteousness and holiness, at the best, are nothing in comparison with God's, [Ps.89.6] Psa 89:6. As God is so great and glorious, how can man, who is guilty and impure, appear before him? We need to be born again of water and of the Holy Ghost, and to be bathed again and again in the blood of Christ, that Fountain opened, [Zech.13.1] Zec 13:1. We should be humbled as mean, guilty, polluted creatures, and renounce self-dependence. But our vileness will commend Christ's condescension and love; the riches of his mercy and the power of his grace will be magnified to all eternity by every sinner he redeems.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesJob reproves Bildad.1–4Job acknowledges the power of God.5–14
Job rebukes Bildad (verses 1–4)

Job mocked Bildad's answer.

His words combined irritability with too high an opinion of himself.

Bildad should have offered Job the Almighty's consolations instead of only warnings of terror.

Jesus Christ knows how to speak the right word to a weary person (Isaiah 50:4).

His ministers should not needlessly distress someone whom God has not intended to make sorrowful.

We are often disappointed by people from whom we expected help and consolation.

But the Holy Spirit, the Comforter, never makes a mistake or fails to accomplish his purpose.

Job describes divine power (verses 5–14)

Job gave striking examples of God's wisdom and power in creating and preserving the world.

Look around at earth and water and you see divine power.

Think of hell beneath, though it is hidden from our sight, and consider how God's power is made known even there.

Look up at heaven and you see further displays of his might.

Through his eternal Spirit, who moved over the waters, and through the breath of his word, God not only made the heavens but adorned them (Psalm 33:6).

Yet the work of redemption surpasses every other marvelous work of God.

Through it we can draw near to him, taste his grace, learn to love him and delight in his commands.

The central disagreement between Job and his friends was their belief that his afflictions proved he had committed exceptionally grave crimes.

They failed to give adequate consideration to the guilt of original sin and God's gracious purpose in purifying his people.

Job himself also spoke about things beyond his understanding.

Yet his view was clearer than theirs.

He does not appear to have claimed his personal righteousness as the ground of his hope before God.

However, by continually describing his sufferings as undeserved and excessively severe, he practically contradicted what he had acknowledged about human sin.

Those complaints showed why the Lord was further humbling him.
classic_reading:
[Job.26.1-Job.26.4]
Chapter 26
Chapter Outline
Job reproves Bildad. | (1-4) |
Job acknowledges the power of God. | (5-14) |
Verses 1-4
Job derided Bildad's answer; his words were a mixture of peevishness and self-preference. Bildad ought to have laid before Job the consolations, rather than the terrors of the Almighty. Christ knows how to speak what is proper for the weary, [Isa.50.4] Is 50:4; and his ministers should not grieve those whom God would not have made sad. We are often disappointed in our expectations from our friends who should comfort us; but the Comforter, the Holy Ghost, never mistakes, nor fails of his end.
[Job.26.5-Job.26.14]
Verses 5-14
Many striking instances are here given of the wisdom and power of God, in the creation and preservation of the world. If we look about us, to the earth and waters here below, we see his almighty power. If we consider hell beneath, though out of our sight, yet we may conceive the discoveries of God's power there. If we look up to heaven above, we see displays of God's almighty power. By his Spirit, the eternal Spirit that moved upon the face of the waters, the breath of his mouth, [Ps.33.6] Psa 33:6, he has not only made the heavens, but beautified them. By redemption, all the other wonderful works of the Lord are eclipsed; and we may draw near, and taste his grace, learn to love him, and walk with delight in his ways. The ground of the controversy between Job and the other disputants was, that they unjustly thought from his afflictions that he must have been guilty of heinous crimes. They appear not to have duly considered the evil and just desert of original sin; nor did they take into account the gracious designs of God in purifying his people. Job also darkened counsel by words without knowledge. But his views were more distinct. He does not appear to have alleged his personal righteousness as the ground of his hope towards God. Yet what he admitted in a general view of his case, he in effect denied, while he complained of his sufferings as unmerited and severe; that very complaint proving the necessity for their being sent, in order to his being further humbled in the sight of God.

Job maintains his sincerity (verses 1–6)

Job's friends finally let him speak without interruption.

He continued with gravity and useful instruction.

Job trusted in both the justice of his cause and the goodness of his God.

He willingly entrusted his case to him.

Yet Job did not show proper reverence when he said God had denied him justice and afflicted his soul.

Holding firmly to our integrity, while resolving not to give our conscience reason to accuse us, frustrates the evil one's designs.

The hypocrite has no secure hope (verses 7–10)

Job considered the position of hypocrites and wicked people deeply miserable.

Even if an insincere profession of religion brought them advantages throughout life, and they held on to false confidence until death, what good would that do when God required their souls?

The more genuine comfort we find in religion, the more firmly we cling to it.

People who find no delight in God are readily drawn away by the pleasures of this life and overcome by its difficulties.

The final ruin of the wicked (<reference osisRef="Job.27.11-Job.27.23" resp="BibleResourcesOriginalSourceRangeInModernSectionHeading">verses 11–23</reference>)

Job's friends had described the worldly suffering of wicked people as always matching the severity of their sins.

Job considered that even if that does not happen, the outcome after death is dreadful.

He therefore presented a truer view of the matter.

For a godly person, death is like a favorable wind carrying a ship toward a heavenly homeland.

For an unrepentant sinner, it is like a storm driving the person toward destruction.

During life, such a sinner benefits from God's patient mercy.

But death ends that period of patience, and God pours out his wrath.

When the Lord brings someone down, no one can flee from or withstand his anger.

Those who refuse now to flee to the arms of divine grace, stretched out to receive them, will not escape the arms of divine wrath, stretched out to destroy them.

What good is it to gain the entire world and lose one's own soul?

Job undertook to set this matter in a true light. Death to a godly man, is like a fair gale of wind to convey him to the heavenly country; but, to a wicked man, it is like a storm, that hurries him away to destruction. While he lived, he had the benefit of sparing mercy; but now the day of God's patience is over, and he will pour out upon him his wrath. When God casts down a man, there is no flying from, nor bearing up under his anger. Those who will not now flee to the arms of Divine grace, which are stretched out to receive them, will not be able to flee from the arms of Divine wrath, which will shortly be stretched out to destroy them. And what is a man profited if he gain the whole world, and thus lose his own soul?

Human beings search for earthly riches (verses 1–11)

Job argued that God's Providence is governed by perfect wisdom.

To illustrate this, he described the extraordinary knowledge and wealth people can gain.

People can discover hidden caverns and minerals beneath the earth, yet they cannot uncover God's hidden counsels in heaven.

Look at miners, those who grow lazy in religion, and learn from their courage and diligence.

They labor intensely for treasures that will perish.

Should their example not shame our indifference and discouragement in seeking true, eternal riches?

Wisdom is better than gold—and safer and easier to obtain in the way God provides.

Yet people pursue gold while neglecting grace.

Why should the uncertain hope of earthly treasure motivate such effort while the certain promise of heavenly riches fails to move us?

Wisdom is worth more than wealth (verses 12–19)

Job spoke of wisdom as knowing God and ourselves, and enjoying fellowship with him.

Its worth is infinitely greater than every earthly treasure.

It is the gift of the Holy Spirit and cannot be bought with money.

We should esteem most highly whatever God esteems most.

Job sought wisdom as someone who sincerely desired to find it, knowing that it was found in God alone, and by means of his revelation.

God gives true wisdom (<reference osisRef="Job.28.20-Job.28.28" resp="BibleResourcesOriginalSourceRangeInModernSectionHeading">verses 20–28</reference>)

There are two kinds of wisdom.

One is hidden within God and is his secret knowledge, which does not belong to us.

The other is revealed by him so that human beings may understand and obey.

Even the events of a single day and a single person's affairs are connected in ways that only God can see fully.

Only the One who sees all at once can judge each part rightly.

But knowledge of God's revealed will is available to us and will do us good.

Let everyone regard this as true wisdom:

Fear the Lord and turn away from evil.

Someone who learns that has learned what matters most.

Where is such wisdom found?

Its treasures are hidden in Jesus Christ, revealed in Scripture, received through faith and communicated by the Holy Spirit.

It will not feed our pride, flatter vanity or satisfy empty curiosity.

Instead it teaches and encourages sinners toward reverence for God, repentance and faith.

It does this without requiring us to solve all the mysteries of this life's events.

Job remembers former comfort (verses 1–6)

Job contrasted his earlier prosperity with his present misery, when he felt that God's comforting presence had been withdrawn.

A soul governed by grace rejoices more in God's favor than in the world's approval.

Job had once enjoyed four particular blessings.

First, confidence in God's protection.

Second, the enjoyment of God's favor.

Third, fellowship with God's word.

Fourth, assurance of God's presence.

God's presence can turn even a small cottage into a fortress and palace.

Job had also enjoyed happiness in his family.

But wealth and flourishing households can be extinguished as quickly as a candle.

When the Holy Spirit enlightens the mind and people live in the light of God's countenance, every outward comfort is doubled and every difficulty becomes easier to bear.

This light guides them cheerfully through life and through death.

Yet the conscious comfort of God's presence may be withdrawn for a time.

Often this follows spiritual neglect or grieving the Holy Spirit.

Sometimes it is instead a test of faith and grace.

We should examine ourselves, seek the cause through earnest prayer and become more watchful.

Job recalls his public usefulness (verses 7–17)

People of every social rank had honored Job, not merely because of his position but because of his wisdom, honesty, integrity and good management.

Those endowed with such abilities have great opportunities to honor God and serve others.

They must also guard carefully against pride.

A community blessed with good leaders has reason for gratitude.

Job's own measure of the value of his prosperous life was his usefulness.

He restrained violent and arrogant people and protected the vulnerable.

Good public officials should similarly hold back evildoers and defend innocent people, using courage and determination.

Such people are blessings to society.

They resemble the Savior, who rescues poor sinners from Satan.

How many who were about to perish now bless him!

Let us trust his mercy and imitate his truth, justice and love.

Job recalls his expectation of a peaceful old age (verses 18–25)

Because Job was respected and useful, he expected to die in peace and honor at an advanced age.

Such hope is good when it grows from active faith in God's promises and Providence.

But if it rests upon confidence in our own wisdom or in changeable earthly circumstances, the foundation is wrong and becomes sinful.

Not everyone who has wisdom is gifted for leadership.

Job had both wisdom and the ability to govern.

He also possessed a tender heart that could console other people.

Those memories were precious to him now that he was mourning.

Jesus Christ is the true King who hates wickedness and upon whom the blessing of a world ready to perish rests.

Let us listen to him.

Verses 1-6
Job proceeds to contrast his former prosperity with his present misery, through God's withdrawing from him. A gracious soul delights in God's smiles, not in the smiles of this world. Four things were then very pleasant to holy Job. 1. The confidence he had in the Divine protection. 2. The enjoyment he had of the Divine favour. 3. The communion he had with the Divine word. 4. The assurance he had of the Divine presence. God's presence with a man in his house, though it be but a cottage, makes it a castle and a palace. Then also he had comfort in his family. Riches and flourishing families, like a candle, may be soon extinguished. But when the mind is enlightened by the Holy Spirit, when a man walks in the light of God's countenance, every outward comfort is doubled, every trouble is diminished, and he may pass cheerfully by this light through life and through death. Yet the sensible comfort of this state is often withdrawn for a season; and commonly this arises from sinful neglect, and grieving the Holy Spirit: sometimes it may be a trial of a man's faith and grace. But it is needful to examine ourselves, to seek for the cause of such a change by fervent prayer, and to increase our watchfulness.
[Job.29.7-Job.29.17]
Verses 7-17
All sorts of people paid respect to Job, not only for the dignity of his rank, but for his personal merit, his prudence, integrity, and good management. Happy the men who are blessed with such gifts as these! They have great opportunities of honouring God and doing good, but have great need to watch against pride. Happy the people who are blessed with such men! it is a token for good to them. Here we see what Job valued himself by, in the day of his prosperity. It was by his usefulness. He valued himself by the check he gave to the violence of proud and evil men. Good magistrates must thus be a restraint to evil-doers, and protect the innocent; in order to this, they should arm themselves with zeal and resolution. Such men are public blessings, and resemble Him who rescues poor sinners from Satan. How many who were ready to perish, now are blessing Him! But who can show forth His praises? May we trust in His mercy, and seek to imitate His truth, justice, and love.
[Job.29.18-Job.29.25]
Verses 18-25
Being thus honoured and useful, Job had hoped to die in peace and honour, in a good old age. If such an expectation arise from lively faith in the providence and promise of God, it is well; but if from conceit of our own wisdom, and dependence on changeable, earthly things, it is ill grounded, and turns to sin. Every one that has the spirit of wisdom, has not the spirit of government; but Job had both. Yet he had the tenderness of a comforter. This he thought upon with pleasure, when he was himself a mourner. Our Lord Jesus is a King who hates iniquity, and upon whom the blessing of a world ready to perish comes. To Him let us give ear.

Job's honor becomes contempt (verses 1–14)

Job compared his present humiliation with the respect and authority he once enjoyed.

How little reason anyone has to become ambitious or proud of earthly honors when they can disappear so easily!

How foolish to place our ultimate confidence in them!

When wicked people despise, insult or hate us, we should not become overwhelmed.

Look instead to Jesus Christ, who endured the hostility of sinners against himself.

Job struggles under inward and outward suffering (verses 15–31)

Job complained bitterly.

At this point, his most persistent sin was cherishing harsh thoughts about God.

When inward temptations are added to outward calamities, the soul can become like a ship tossed in a storm, full of confusion and distress.

Yet how dreadful is the position of people who truly have God as an enemy!

Compared with the eternal ruin awaiting unrepentant sinners, what are even the most severe outward or inward sufferings of this present life?

Job found some comfort, though little.

He expected death to end his trials.

God's wrath might bring him to death, but his soul would be safe and happy in the world of spirits.

Even if no human being pities us, God both corrects and pities his children, as a father does.

Let us direct our thoughts more toward eternity.

There the believer's mourning will end and be replaced by joyful praise for redeeming love.

Verses 1-14
Job contrasts his present condition with his former honour and authority. What little cause have men to be ambitious or proud of that which may be so easily lost, and what little confidence is to be put in it! We should not be cast down if we are despised, reviled, and hated by wicked men. We should look to Jesus, who endured the contradiction of sinners.
[Job.30.15-Job.30.31]
Verses 15-31
Job complains a great deal. Harbouring hard thoughts of God was the sin which did, at this time, most easily beset Job. When inward temptations join with outward calamities, the soul is hurried as in a tempest, and is filled with confusion. But woe be to those who really have God for an enemy! Compared with the awful state of ungodly men, what are all outward, or even inward temporal afflictions? There is something with which Job comforts himself, yet it is but a little. He foresees that death will be the end of all his troubles. God's wrath might bring him to death; but his soul would be safe and happy in the world of spirits. If none pity us, yet our God, who corrects, pities us, even as a father pitieth his own children. And let us look more to the things of eternity: then the believer will cease from mourning, and joyfully praise redeeming love.
